title: About Camden
text:
Camden Rine
 Sports Media & Communication | University of Nebraska–Lincoln
I am an aspiring professional in sports media and communication with a passion for basketball, analytics, coaching, athlete development, and the emerging world of NIL. I am currently pursuing a Bachelor of Journalism in Sports Media and Communication with a minor in Coaching at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln and set to graduate in December 2025.
Through multiple hands-on experiences in various sports, I have built a background that blends media and coaching. I have served as a student manager for the Nebraska Men’s Basketball Team, gaining firsthand experience in player development, scouting, and team operations at the Division I level. My contributions over four years contributed to two championships, the 2025 inaugural College Basketball Crown in Las Vegas and the 2024 Diamond Head Classic in Honolulu.
I have also worked as a scout for Prep Network and NXTPRO Sports, providing in-depth player evaluations and performance reports for high school and collegiate athletes. As well as working in basketball, I spent the Summer of 2025 working for the Lincoln Saltdogs as a Clubhouse Manager, gaining more experience with athlete development and coordination.

title: Are the 2023-24 Boston Celtics the Best Offensive Team of All Time?
text:
The 2023-24 Boston Celtics season was not just dominant, it was historic. The Celtics utilized math and analytics to secure one of the most dominant championship runs in recent NBA history. The Celtics posted an offensive rating over 122 by the season’s end, which is the highest in NBA history by far. Offensive rating is a statistic that measures a team’s offensive efficiency by calculating the points scored over 100 possessions. This is an important metric because when comparing teams from different decades, this can take into account the pace of play. When comparing the 2023-24 Celtics to other all-time great teams like the 1995-96 Chicago Bulls or the 2016-17 Warriors, the numbers make it clear, the Celtics didn’t just score more than everyone else, they changed how basketball was played.
Chart 1


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggalt)
library(ggtext)
library(gt)

offense <- read_csv("celticsOrtg.csv") 
top20 <- offense |> 
  filter(
    ORtg > 114.6
  )

bulls <- top20 |>
  filter(
    Team == "1995-96CHI"
  )

warriors <- top20 |>
  filter(
    Team == "2016-17GSW"
    
  )
celtics <- top20 |>
  filter(
    Team == "2023-24BOS"
  )
ggplot() + 
  geom_bar(data=top20, aes(x=reorder(Team, ORtg), weight=ORtg), fill = "lightgrey") +
  geom_bar(data=bulls, aes(x=reorder(Team, ORtg), weight=ORtg), fill = "#CE1141") +
  geom_bar(data=warriors, aes(x=reorder(Team, ORtg), weight=ORtg), fill = "#1D428A") +
  geom_bar(data=celtics, aes(x=reorder(Team, ORtg), weight=ORtg), fill = "#007A33") +
  coord_flip() +
      labs(
    x="Season and Team", 
    y="Offensive Rating", 
    title="The 23-24 Boston Celtics Had the Best Offensive Season in NBA History", 
    subtitle="How do the Celtics stack up against other all-time greats?", 
    caption="Source: Basketball Reference | By Camden Rine"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    
  )









The 2023-24 Celtics show that they are towering above all other all-time offensive juggernauts. When looking at why this is, it is because of their line-ups. They used balance and spacing. Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown obviously carried the offensive load, but what is interesting is the supporting cast. Every player they put on the court was a highly capable three-point shooter. With guys like Kristaps Porziņģis and Al Horford, who are usually your “big men,” always roaming around the three-point line with exceptional spacing, always being a threat from behind the arc, defenses were always on their toes, knowing they had to treat everyone like a sharp shooter. While the 2016-17 Warriors revolutionized spacing and shooting, the 2023-24 Celtics perfected it.
Chart 2
Now let’s take a look at three-point volume, the heart of this transformation, in my opinion. Shown are the top 20 teams of all-time in three-point attempts and how many they made.


Code
threeattempts <- read_csv("celtics3pa.csv")

top20attempts <- threeattempts |> 
  filter(
    `3PA` > 2560
  )

ggplot() + 
  geom_dumbbell(
    data=top20attempts, 
    aes(y=Team, x=`3PA`, xend=`3P`),
        size = 2,
    colour = "gray",
    colour_x = "green",
    colour_xend = "blue") +
  labs(
    x = "Threes Made vs Threes Attempted",
    title="The Celtics are Changing the Game of Basketball", 
    subtitle = "<span style = 'color:blue;'>Threes made</span> in a single season are on the left. <span style = 'color:green;'>Threes attempted</span> are on the right consisting of teams with the most threes attempted in a season.",
    caption="Source: Basketball Reference | By Camden Rine"
  ) + 
  theme(
    plot.subtitle = element_textbox_simple()
  )









The 2023-24 Boston Celtics actually did not shoot the most threes in NBA history. Surprising? Maybe, but when you look at the two teams ahead of them, it’s the Celtics from the year before, and the year after! This further shows how far they have taken this three-point revolution. So yes, everyone has seen how successful the Celtics have been with the three-point shot the past three years, so then the question is, why haven’t other teams tried this analytical strategy? Well, they have, the two teams at the top of the dumbbell chart, the 2024-25 Cavaliers and eventual champion Thunder, shot and made near the most threes of all time as well! This further shows that the Celtics have seriously changed the NBA as everyone knows it.
Chart 3


Code
ts <- read_csv("celticsts%.csv")

topts <- ts |> 
  filter( `TS%` > 0.588 ) |> 
  select(Team, `TS%`, `eFG%`, `FG%`)

topts |> 
  gt() |> 
  cols_label(
    `TS%` = "True Shooting Percentage",
    `eFG%` = "Effective Field Goal Percentage",
    `FG%` = "Field Goal Percentage"
  ) |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Are the 2023-24 Boston Celtics the best shooting team of all time as well?",
    subtitle = "The 2023-24 Celtics have the best true shooting percentage in a season of all time."
  ) |> tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", weight = "bold", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("title")
  ) |> tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("subtitle")
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = md("**By:** Camden Rine  |  **Source:** Basketball Reference")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
     locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything()),
     style = list(
       cell_borders(sides = "bottom", weight = px(4)),
       cell_text(weight = "bold", size=13)
     )
   ) |>
  opt_row_striping() |> 
  opt_table_lines("none") |>
    fmt_percent(
    columns = c(`TS%`, `eFG%`, `FG%`),
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_fill(color = "#007A33"),
      cell_text(color = "black")
      ),
    locations = cells_body(
      rows = Team == "2023-24BOS")
  )

Looking above this basically ties everything together, showing how much the Celtics’ strategy paid off. With the best true shooting percentage season in NBA history at 60.9%, and an effective field goal percentage of 57.8%, the 2023-24 Boston Celtics combined record volume, with record efficiency. That is the balance that no team before has ever been able to replicate, shooting and making more shots than anyone in history.
This Celtics team didn’t just have a great year, they had THE year. They created a blueprint for the modern NBA as we know it. Teams league-wide have scrambled to study their spacing, roster construction, and shot selection patterns in hopes of having near the success they did. The Celtics did something no team has been able to perfect before, using analytics and math to their advantage, proving that smart basketball can be beautiful basketball, too.
Data from : https://www.basketball-reference.com/

title: Did Jayson Tatum Get Snubbed of Finals MVP in 2023-24?
text:
While the 2023-24 NBA Finals was a long time coming and huge celebration for Celtics fans, it sparked up an interesting debate in a time of success. Should Jayson Tatum of won the Finals MVP over Jaylen Brown? While Brown ultimately took home the award, the stats and overall impact make the conversation a lot more complicated than it may appear.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(waffle)
library(ggrepel)
library(ggbump)
library(gt)

avg <- read_csv("Project 2 Data - FinalsAverages.csv")

JB <- avg |>
  filter(
    NAME == "Jaylen Brown 23-24"
  )
Pierce <- avg |>
  filter(
    NAME == "Paul Pierce 07-08"
  )
SGA <- avg |>
  filter(
    NAME == "Shai Gilgeous-Alexander 24-25"
  )
Joker <- avg |>
  filter(
    NAME == "Nikola Jokić 22-23"
  )

ggplot() + 
  geom_bar(data=avg, aes(x=reorder(NAME, PPG), weight=PPG), fill = "lightgrey") +
  geom_bar(data=JB, aes(x=reorder(NAME, PPG), weight=PPG), fill = "#008348") +
  geom_bar(data=Pierce, aes(x=reorder(NAME, PPG), weight=PPG), fill = "#008348") +
  geom_bar(data=SGA, aes(x=reorder(NAME, PPG), weight=PPG), fill = "blue") +
  geom_bar(data=Joker, aes(x=reorder(NAME, PPG), weight=PPG), fill = "yellow") +
  coord_flip() +
      labs(
    x="Season and Player", 
    y="Points Per Game in Finals", 
    title="Where Does The Actual Winner Jaylen Brown, Stack up Against the Rest?", 
    subtitle="Why is Brown so much lower compared to previous winners?", 
    caption="Source: Basketball Reference and StatMuse | By Camden Rine"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    
  )









This first puts Jaylen Brown’s scoring into context compared to other Finals MVP winners in the modern era. What immediately stands out is Brown’s point average is far below previous winners. Most winners of the award sit around that 24-30 points per game threshold, which Brown is below.
This does not mean Brown is not deserving of the award by any means, but it helps explain why many people argued that Jayson Tatum may have had the overall stronger case. This also potentially shows that the Celtics won in a year where they were incredibly balanced. The scoring load was spread between many players, because of that, traditional MVP scoring standards might not apply.


Code
totalpoints <- c("Tatum"=111, "Brown"=104)
totalrebounds <- c("Tatum"=39, "Brown"=23)
totalassists <- c("Tatum"=36, "Brown"=15)
iron(
  waffle(
  totalpoints/3, 
  rows = 5,
  colors = c("black", "#008348")) + 
  labs(
  x="1 Square = 3 Points",
     title="Tatum vs. Brown: By The Numbers", 
     subtitle="Tatum surpassed Brown in all major catagories.") + 
   theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 19, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title.y = element_blank()
  ),
 waffle(
   totalrebounds, 
        rows = 5,
   x = "1 Square = 1 Rebound",
        colors = c("black", "#008348")
        ),
 waffle(
   totalassists, 
   rows = 5, 
   colors = c("black", "#008348", "white")) + 
   labs(
     x = "1 Square = 1 Assist",
     caption="Source: Basketball Reference and StatMuse | Graphic by Camden Rine"
     )
) 









This really breaks down the debate into its simplest form. Who had more points, rebounds and assists? Here the results are pretty hard to ignore, Jayson Tatum is ahead of Brown in every major statistical category. What this really signifies is how much more responsibility Tatum had to carry across the whole Finals. He had to lead the team in rebounding and assists, while also being expected to score the most, which he did all of these.


Code
gamebygame <- read_csv("Project 2 Data - BrownvTatumbygame copy.csv")
  ggplot() + 
  geom_bump(data=gamebygame, aes(x=Game, y=PTS, color=Player)) +
    geom_point(data=gamebygame, aes(x=Game, y=PTS, color=Player), size = 4) +
     scale_color_manual(values = c(
  "black",
  "#008348")) +
    labs(
    x="Finals Game", 
    y="Points", 
    title="Jayson Tatum Starts Slow But Steps Up When It Matters ", 
    subtitle="Jaylen Brown started hot, but Tatum took over in the late stages", 
    caption="Source: Basketball Reference and StatMuse | By Camden Rine"
    ) +
  theme_minimal()









While this looks simple, this highlights one of the biggest storylines of the Finals and of Jayson Tatum’s career as a whole. A lot of NBA media and NBA Twitter think that Jayson Tatum “chokes” in big moments. This chart completely disproves that, Tatum stepped up biggest when it mattered most. While Brown had a better start than Tatum, Tatum continually got better throughout the series, as well as a stellar title-clinching game five. This late-series surge by Tatum is important because while Finals MVP often comes down to overall production and numbers, it also comes down to clutch moments and games, which I think the edge clearly goes to Tatum. When the stakes rose, Tatum elevated his game to the next level.


Code
tatumvbrown <- read_csv("Project 2 Data - TatumvBrownAverages.csv")

wantedstats <- tatumvbrown |> 
  select(Name, PPG, MPG, RPG, SPG, APG, BPG, FGA, `FG%`, `3PA`, `3P%`, `TS%`, TOV, PLUSMINUS)

wantedstats |> 
gt() |> 
  cols_label(
    `TS%` = "True Shooting Percentage",
    PPG = "Points",
    MPG = "Minutes",
    RPG = "Rebounds",
    SPG = "Steals",
    APG = "Assists",
    BPG = "Blocks",
    FGA = "Shots",
    `3PA` = "Threes Attempted",
    TOV = "Turnovers",
    PLUSMINUS = "Plus/Minus"
  ) |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Tatum Looks Like the Better Candidate",
    subtitle = "Jayson Tatum surpasses Jaylen brown in many statistical averages, what about efficiency?"
  ) |> tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", weight = "bold", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("title")
  ) |> tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("subtitle")
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = md("**By:** Camden Rine  |  **Source:** Basketball Reference and StatMuse")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
     locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything()),
     style = list(
       cell_borders(sides = "bottom", weight = px(4)),
       cell_text(weight = "bold", size=13)
     )
   ) |>
  opt_row_striping() |> 
  opt_table_lines("none") |>
 tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_fill(color = "#008348"),
      cell_text(color = "white")
      ),
    locations = cells_body(
      rows = Name == "Jayson Tatum")
  )

This makes the argument even clearer. When you directly line up the statistical profiles Jayson Tatum beats Brown in basically every category. Tatum averaged more points, more rebounds, more assists and more minutes. The glaring thing that stands out here is Tatum’s 7.2 assists per game. This is an astonishing number to have while also being the first scoring option, as he was creating offense in a multitude of ways throughout the series.
Brown actually has a slight edge in the efficiency metrics as well as more steals and blocks, but the overall picture still largely favors Tatum. Tatum took more shots, handled more possessions and was asked to do much more in Boston’s offense. Tatum’s combination of scoring and facilitating show an overall more complete Final’s performance.
Looking at the numbers, trends and visuals together, it seems clear why many people think Jayson Tatum was deserving of the Finals MVP over Jaylen Brown. Brown had some important moments in Game 1 and 2, but Tatum took over later in the series and really put the nail in the coffin on the Mavericks. With all the data considered, this has a chance to go up there with one of the biggest Finals MVP snubs of all time.
